name: Horseshoe moustache

lead: The horseshoe moustache is a full moustache whose ends run straight down from the corners of the mouth to the jawline, forming an upside-down U. It is also called the biker moustache and differs from the Fu Manchu, whose ends hang past the chin.

Wearers use it to frame the lower face and add a strong, masculine outline, and it is associated with Hulk Hogan and with cowboy, biker and wrestling imagery. Studies on facial hair generally link it to perceptions of masculinity and dominance.

paras: It is grown for several months, combed downward as it lengthens, kept clean and conditioned, and shaped by trimming the outline of the extensions, with regular maintenance to hold the shape.
There are no health risks beyond ordinary skin irritation from grooming products. Style choices carry social associations that vary by setting.

angle.text: The style adds a strong outline around the mouth and chin sides. It suits men who can grow dense facial hair and want a rugged look.

lead: The horseshoe moustache is a full moustache with extensions running vertically from the corners of the lips down to the jawline, producing an inverted U. It is also known as the biker moustache, and may have been popularised by modern cowboys.[1]

People use it as a style choice that outlines the mouth and lower face and signals ruggedness; it is associated with Hulk Hogan, and with Sam Elliott, Axl Rose and Paul Teutul Sr.[2] Moustaches generally date back to ancient Egypt, and they were fashionable in the West through the late nineteenth century.[3]

paras: The style is a full moustache with thick extensions from the mouth corners toward the jaw. By contrast, the Fu Manchu has long drooping ends that extend past the chin, and the handlebar has small upturned ends.[1]

One account places its emergence among cowboys and outlaws of the nineteenth-century American West, with later popularity among bikers and working-class men, a rise in the 1970s through wrestling and rock music, a peak in the 1980s and a decline in the 1990s.[2] Gardner Minshew and Joe Exotic helped revive the style.[1] That account relies on thin sourcing, and the style may have been popularised by cowboys.[1][2]
Growth takes several months. Growers comb it downward, wash and condition it, and define the U-shape by trimming; light wax is sometimes used.[2]
The style is often associated with masculinity, toughness and rebellion, and its meaning has shifted toward nostalgia and irony in modern fashion.[2]

timeline.event: Style grows through wrestling, rock and biker culture.[2]
